title: 火山
summary: 火山は、地下の溶けた岩石の貯留層につながる火口を中心に、噴出した溶岩や火山砕屑物が積み重なってできた地形であり、溶岩やガスが噴出する開口部そのものを指すこともある。マグマに溶け込んだガスの抜けやすさが噴火の様式を左右し、静かな溶岩流から爆発的な灰の噴出まで幅がある。
bodyMarkdown:
## マグマと噴火の仕組み

火山は、地下の溶けた岩石の貯留層につながる火口を中心に築かれた円錐形の丘や山であり、「火山」という語は溶融岩やガスが噴出する開口部そのものを指すこともある。地下で火山の通り道を上昇する溶融岩はマグマと呼ばれ、火山から噴出した後は溶岩と呼ばれる。 [1][2]

溶融岩は周囲の固体岩石より軽く、浮力とガス圧に駆動されて上方へ押し上げられ、地殻の弱い帯域を突き破ると噴火が始まる。上昇するマグマは結晶や周囲の未溶融岩石の破片、溶存ガスを含むが、主体は酸素・ケイ素・アルミニウム・鉄・マグネシウム・カルシウム・ナトリウム・カリウム・チタン・マンガンからなる液体である。 [3][4]

すべてのマグマは溶存ガスを含み、地表へ向かうにつれて周囲の圧力が下がり、ガスは静かにまたは爆発的に放出される。溶岩が薄く流動的であればガスは容易に逃げるが、厚く粘稠であればガスは自由に動けず巨大な圧力が蓄積し、最終的に爆発的に逃げ出す。 [5][6]

ガスと溶岩の激しい分離は軽石と呼ばれる岩石の泡を生じ、泡の多さゆえに水に浮くほど軽いものもある。地表近くで急速に冷えたマグマは結晶の少ない微細質またはガラス質の火成岩となるが、地表に届かず地下深くにとどまったマグマはゆっくり結晶化して粗粒でほぼ完全結晶質の火成岩となり、長い時間を経て侵食により花崗岩質の岩体として露出することがある。 [7][8][9]

## 噴火様式と噴出物

噴火の様式は、噴出するマグマの化学組成・結晶量・温度・溶存ガスと、噴出量・噴出率によって決まる。低粘度の玄武岩質マグマでは溶岩流や溶岩噴泉が主で灰はほとんど出ないのに対し、粘性が高くガスに富む流紋岩質・デイサイト質マグマでは、大量の灰を成層圏高くまで注入する極端に爆発的な噴火となる。 [23]

爆発的噴火は、溶けた岩石に溶け込んだガスが上昇とともに膨張して激しく空中へ逃げる場合や、水がマグマに熱せられて急激に水蒸気へ変わる場合に起こる。 [25]

火山灰は燃焼の産物ではなく、直径2ミリから0.004ミリ未満までの岩石・鉱物・火山ガラスの破片からなり、硬く研磨性があり、弱い腐食性を持ち、湿ると電気を通し、水に溶けない。微細な噴出物は風によって遠くまで運ばれ、最も細かい灰は成層圏の風に乗って地球を何周もしてから降着することがある。 [20][21][22][26]

## 火山の主な種類

地質学者は火山を一般に、スコリア丘、成層火山、楯状火山、溶岩ドームの4種類に分類する。 [10]

スコリア丘は最も単純な火山で、単一の火口から噴出して固化した溶岩片が火口の周辺に降り積もってできる円形または楕円形の丘であり、山頂に椀状の火口を持ち、周囲より1,000フィート余り以上高くなることはまれである。1943年にはメキシコのパリクティン村近くの農場でスコリア丘が成長を始め、9年間の活動で高さ約1,200フィートの丘を築き、約100平方マイルを灰で覆い、サンファンの町を破壊した。 [11][12][13]

成層火山（複式火山）は溶岩流・火山灰・スコリア・岩塊・火山弾の互層からなる急斜面で対称的な大円錐で、麓から8,000フィートもそびえることがあり、富士山やレーニア山などが代表例である。楯状火山はほぼ完全に流動性の高い溶岩流で築かれ、戦士の盾に似た幅広くなだらかな円錐をなし、最大級の例であるマウナロアは海抜13,677フィートだが、山頂は深い海底から28,000フィート以上の高さにあたる。 [14][15][16]

溶岩ドームは粘性が高く遠くまで流れられない溶岩が火口の上や周囲に盛り上がってでき、主に内部からの膨張によって成長する。火山の頂部が崩壊してできるカルデラは、直径1〜15マイルのほぼ円形の窪地から長さ60マイルにもなる細長い窪地まであり、オレゴン州のクレーターレイクは約6,800年前の一連の大爆発の後に頂部が崩壊して水をたたえた例である。 [17][18][19]

## 噴火の被害と関連する現象

噴出物は火山地形を築く一方で、壊滅的な被害ももたらす。1902年にマルティニーク島のモン・ペレでは、溶岩ドームの成長を伴う噴火による白熱した高速の灰流と熱いガス・火山塵が、約4マイル下流のサンピエールの町を壊滅させ、約3万人の住民が死亡した。 [24]

火山活動は[プレートテクトニクス](/hubpedia/plate-tectonics)が扱うプレート境界の運動と密接に結びつき、噴火の前後には[地震](/hubpedia/earthquake)を伴い、山体の一部が崩れて[地すべり](/hubpedia/landslide)を起こすこともある。噴火の様式を決めるのはあくまでマグマの物性であり、流出型か爆発型かで被害の姿も変わる。 [23]

en.title: Volcano
en.summary: A volcano is a landform built around a vent that connects with reservoirs of molten rock below the Earth's surface, as erupted lava and fragmental material accumulate; the term can also refer to the opening itself through which molten rock and gases are expelled. How easily gases dissolved in magma can escape controls the style of an eruption, which ranges from quiet lava flows to explosive ejection of ash.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Magma and how eruptions begin

A volcano is most commonly a conical hill or mountain built around a vent that connects with reservoirs of molten rock below the surface of the Earth, and the term volcano can also refer to the opening through which the molten rock and associated gases are expelled. Molten rock that rises through volcanic vents below the surface is known as magma; after it erupts from a volcano it is called lava. [1][2]

Molten rock is lighter than the surrounding solid rock and, driven by buoyancy and gas pressure, forces its way upward; when it ultimately breaks through zones of weakness in the Earth's crust, an eruption begins. Ascending magma commonly contains some crystals, fragments of unmelted surrounding rocks, and dissolved gases, but it is primarily a liquid composed principally of oxygen, silicon, aluminum, iron, magnesium, calcium, sodium, potassium, titanium, and manganese. [3][4]

All magmas contain dissolved gases, and as they rise to the surface to erupt, the confining pressures are reduced and the dissolved gases are liberated either quietly or explosively. If the lava is a thin fluid, the gases may escape easily, but if the lava is thick and pasty, the gases cannot move freely, build up tremendous pressure, and ultimately escape with explosive violence. [5][6]

The violent separation of gas from lava may produce a rock froth called pumice, some of which is so light, because of the many gas bubbles, that it floats on water. Magmas that cool rapidly near or on the Earth's surface solidify into finely crystalline or glassy igneous rocks with few crystals, while magmas that never breach the surface cool much more slowly and become coarser grained, nearly completely crystalline igneous rocks that erosion can later expose as large granitic bodies. [7][8][9]

## Eruption styles and erupted material

The style of a volcanic eruption is controlled by the characteristics of the erupting magma and the volume of and rate at which the magma is emitted. Eruptions of low-viscosity basaltic magma are typified by effusion of lava flows and lava fountains that produce very little ash, whereas highly viscous, gas-rich rhyolite and dacite magmas produce extremely explosive eruptions that inject large quantities of ash high into the stratosphere. [23]

Explosive eruptions occur when gases dissolved in molten rock expand as the magma rises and then escape violently into the air, or when water is heated by magma and abruptly flashes into steam. [25]

Volcanic ash is not the product of combustion but consists of fragments of rocks, minerals, and volcanic glass ranging from 2 mm down to less than 0.004 mm in diameter; it is hard, abrasive, mildly corrosive, conducts electricity when wet, and does not dissolve in water. Fine ejected material is carried far by wind, and the finest ash particles may be injected miles into the atmosphere and carried many times around the world by stratospheric winds before settling out. [20][21][22][26]

## Principal types of volcanoes

Geologists generally group volcanoes into four main kinds: cinder cones, composite volcanoes, shield volcanoes, and lava domes. [10]

Cinder cones are the simplest type of volcano, built from particles and blobs of congealed lava ejected from a single vent into a circular or oval cone; most have a bowl-shaped crater at the summit and rarely rise more than a thousand feet above their surroundings. In 1943 a cinder cone started growing on a farm near the village of Paricutin in Mexico, and during 9 years of activity it built a prominent cone about 1,200 feet high, covered about 100 square miles with ash, and destroyed the town of San Juan. [11][12][13]

Composite volcanoes, also called stratovolcanoes, are steep-sided, symmetrical cones of large dimension built of alternating layers of lava flows, volcanic ash, cinders, blocks, and bombs, and may rise as much as 8,000 feet above their bases; Mount Fuji and Mount Rainier are among the representative examples. Shield volcanoes are built almost entirely of fluid lava flows into a broad, gently sloping cone with a profile much like a warrior's shield, and Mauna Loa, the largest of them, projects 13,677 feet above sea level while its top stands over 28,000 feet above the deep ocean floor. [14][15][16]

Lava domes are formed by relatively small, bulbous masses of lava too viscous to flow any great distance, piling over and around the vent and growing largely by expansion from within. Calderas, the steep-walled depressions formed by collapse of volcanoes, range from roughly circular depressions 1 to 15 miles in diameter to huge elongated depressions as much as 60 miles long; Crater Lake in Oregon formed when a volcano lost its top following a series of tremendous explosions about 6,800 years ago and the collapsed depression later filled with water. [17][18][19]

## Eruption damage and related phenomena

Erupted material builds volcanic terrain but also brings devastating damage. In 1902 at Mont Pelee on Martinique, an eruption accompanying the growth of a lava dome sent an incandescent, high-velocity ash flow and associated hot gases and volcanic dust into the coastal town of St. Pierre about 4 miles downslope to the south, demolishing the town and killing nearly 30,000 inhabitants. [24]

Volcanic activity is closely tied to the plate-boundary motions described by [plate tectonics](/hubpedia/plate-tectonics), eruptions can be accompanied by [earthquakes](/hubpedia/earthquake), and part of an edifice can collapse as a [landslide](/hubpedia/landslide). What fixes the style of an eruption remains the physical character of the magma, and whether the eruption is effusive or explosive changes the shape of the damage. [23]

title: 津波
summary: 津波は、海洋の大規模で突然の変位によって発生する一連の長い波であり、海底の地震を最大の原因とし、地すべり・火山活動・気象・隕石によっても起こりうる。深海では波長が数百マイルに及び目立たないが、浅瀬で減速する代わりに波高が増し、沿岸に洪水と強い海流をもたらす。
bodyMarkdown:
## 津波の定義と原因

津波は、海洋の大規模で突然の変位によって発生する一連の長い波であり、海底の[地震](/hubpedia/earthquake)や海底[火山](/hubpedia/volcano)の噴火によって引き起こされる巨大な波である。海底またはその近くの大地震が最も一般的な原因だが、[地すべり](/hubpedia/landslide)、火山活動、特定の気象、隕石も津波を起こしうる。 [1][19][2]

津波は「潮波」と呼ばれることがあるが、潮汐とは関係がないためこの呼び方は誤解を招き、海洋学者はこの名称を推奨していない。 [3][22]

## 深海での伝播

津波は発生源から全方位へ放射状に広がり、海洋盆地全体を横断することがある。風による波が海洋の表層だけに影響するのと異なり、津波は海面から海底までの水柱全体を通じて伝わる。 [4][13]

津波の速度は、重力加速度（毎秒毎秒32.2フィート、約9.8メートル）と水深の積の平方根で計算でき、発生源からの距離ではなく海洋の深さに依存する。水深15,000フィート（4,600メートル）では時速約475マイル（765キロメートル）になり、深海ではジェット機並みの時速500マイル（800キロメートル）超で進んで1日足らずで大洋全体を横断できる。 [10][20][11][14]

この速さなら、津波はアラスカのアリューシャン列島からハワイまで約5時間、ポルトガル沿岸からノースカロライナまで8時間半で進む。波長は数百マイルにもなるため、深海では高さが3フィート（約1メートル）を超えることはめったになくほとんど目立たず、海上の船員は船体の下を通過する津波に通常気づかない。 [12][15][16]

## 沿岸での増幅と被害

陸に近い浅瀬に入ると津波は減速し、波長が縮み、波高が増し、海流が強まる。岸では多くの津波が自動車並みの時速20〜30マイル（30〜50キロメートル）まで減速する。沿岸に達した津波は、数時間から数日続く危険な沿岸洪水と強い海流を引き起こす。 [17][18][5]

2009年9月29日には、南太平洋の大地震で発生した津波が米領サモア、サモア、トンガに大きな被害と犠牲をもたらした。1850年以降、津波は世界中で数十万人の命を奪い、数千億ドルの被害をもたらしている。 [21][6]

## 名称の由来とリスクの広がり

「津波（ツナミ）」という語は、日本語で「港の波」を意味する文字に由来する。世界のすべての海洋の沿岸に位置するコミュニティは津波のリスクを抱えており、津波は自然界で最も強力で破壊的な力の一つとされる。 [8][9]

海底またはその近くの大地震が最も一般的な原因であり、[プレートテクトニクス](/hubpedia/plate-tectonics)が説明するプレート境界の運動がこうした地震の多くを生み出す。津波はどの海洋沿岸にもいつでも襲来しうるもので、津波に季節はない。 [7]

en.title: Tsunami
en.summary: A tsunami is a series of long waves generated by a large and sudden displacement of the ocean, most commonly caused by earthquakes below or near the ocean floor but also possible from landslides, volcanic activity, certain types of weather, and meteorites. In the deep ocean its wavelengths can be hundreds of miles and it is barely noticeable, but in shallow water it slows and builds in height, bringing coastal flooding and powerful currents.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Definition and causes

A tsunami is a series of long waves generated by a large and sudden displacement of the ocean: giant waves caused by [earthquakes](/hubpedia/earthquake) or [volcanic](/hubpedia/volcano) eruptions under the sea. Large earthquakes below or near the ocean floor are the most common cause, but [landslides](/hubpedia/landslide), volcanic activity, certain types of weather, and meteorites can also cause a tsunami. [1][19][2]

Tsunamis are sometimes referred to as "tidal waves", but this is very misleading because they are not related to tides, and oceanographers discourage the name. [3][22]

## Propagation through the deep ocean

Tsunamis radiate outward in all directions from their source and can move across entire ocean basins. Unlike wind waves that affect just the surface of the ocean, tsunamis propagate through the entire depth of the ocean, from the surface to the floor. [4][13]

Tsunami speed can be computed by taking the square root of the product of the acceleration of gravity, 32.2 feet (9.8 meters) per second squared, and water depth, so it depends on ocean depth rather than the distance from the source of the wave. In 15,000 feet (4,600 meters) of water this works out to almost 475 mph (765 km/h), and in the deep ocean tsunamis can move as fast as a jet plane, over 500 mph (800 km/h), crossing entire oceans in less than a day. [10][20][11][14]

At rates like this, a tsunami will travel from Alaska's Aleutian Islands to Hawaii in about five hours, or from the Portugal coast to North Carolina in eight and a half hours. Because a tsunami's wavelengths can be hundreds of miles, it is barely noticeable in the deep ocean and rarely more than three feet (one meter) high, and mariners at sea will not normally notice a tsunami passing beneath their hulls. [12][15][16]

## Amplification and damage along the coast

As a tsunami enters shallow water near land, it slows down, wavelengths decrease, waves grow in height, and currents intensify. At the shore, most tsunamis slow to the speed of a car, approximately 20 to 30 mph (30 to 50 km/h). When they reach the coast, they can cause dangerous coastal flooding and powerful currents that can last for several hours or days. [17][18][5]

On September 29, 2009, a tsunami generated by a large earthquake in the Southern Pacific Ocean caused substantial damage and loss of life in American Samoa, Samoa, and Tonga. Since 1850, tsunamis have claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and caused hundreds of billions of dollars in damage around the world. [21][6]

## Origin of the name and the spread of risk

The word "tsunami," pronounced soo-NAH-mee, comes from the Japanese characters meaning "harbor wave." Communities along the coasts of all the world's oceans are at risk from tsunamis, which are one of nature's most powerful and destructive forces. [8][9]

Large earthquakes below or near the ocean floor are the most common cause, and the plate-boundary motions explained by [plate tectonics](/hubpedia/plate-tectonics) produce many of those earthquakes. A tsunami can strike any ocean coast at any time; there is no season for tsunamis. [7]

title: プレートテクトニクス
summary: プレートテクトニクスは、地球の最外層が互いに相対的に動く大小12枚以上の硬い岩石のプレートに分かれ、より高温で動きやすい物質の上に乗っているとする理論である。発散・収束・トランスフォームというプレート境界の運動が地震・火山・造山を説明し、1912年のヴェーゲナーの大陸移動説を前身として1960年代に確立された。
bodyMarkdown:
## プレートテクトニクスの理論

地質学でプレートとは硬い固体岩石の大きな板を指し、テクトニクスはギリシャ語で「建てる」を意味する語根に由来する。プレートテクトニクス理論は、地球の最外層が互いに相対的に動く大小12枚以上のプレートに分かれ、より高温で動きやすい物質の上に乗っていると主張する。 [1][2]

この理論が想定する前身として、超大陸パンゲアは約2億2,500万〜2億年前に分裂を始め、現在の大陸へと分かれた。プレートテクトニクスは古生物学から地震学まで地球科学の多くの分野を統合し、[地震](/hubpedia/earthquake)や[火山](/hubpedia/volcano)噴火が世界の特定の地域に集中する理由や、大山脈の成因を説明する枠組みを提供した。 [3][10]

## 大陸移動説からプレートテクトニクスへ

大陸が現在の位置に固定されていないという考えは、1596年にオランダの地図製作者アブラハム・オルテリウスが『テサウルス・ゲオグラフィクス』で早くも示唆していた。移動する大陸が本格的な科学理論として取り上げられたのは1912年で、32歳のドイツの気象学者アルフレート・ローター・ヴェーゲナーが2編の論文で大陸移動説を発表した。 [4][5]

ヴェーゲナーは、南アメリカとアフリカの沿岸部に同一の化石種が見つかることを両大陸のかつての結合の最も有力な証拠と考え、南極で発見された熱帯植物の化石（石炭堆積物の形）や現在の乾燥アフリカの氷河堆積物もその裏付けとされた。 [6]

この理論の致命的弱点は、固体岩石の巨大な塊を大洋底を通して遠距離まで動かしうる力を説明できなかった点で、イギリスの地球物理学者ハロルド・ジェフリーズは、固体岩石の大きな塊が破壊されずに大洋底を押し進むことは物理的に不可能だと正しく論じた。ヴェーゲナーは1930年にグリーンランド氷冠を横断する探検中に凍死したが、彼が巻き起こした論争は続き、没後の海底探査などの新証拠が理論への関心を再燃させてプレートテクトニクスへ発展した。 [7][8]

プレートテクトニクスは地球科学において、物理学・化学における原子構造の発見や生命科学における進化論と同程度に重要であることが証明された。ただし、プレートを推進する力の本性はヴェーゲナーが解決できなかった問いであり、今日も主要な未解決問題の一つであり続けている。 [9][11]

## プレート境界の4つの型

プレートの運動の大部分はプレート間の狭い帯域で起こり、境界には発散・収束・トランスフォーム・境界帯の4種類がある。発散境界はプレートが離れていく拡大中心に沿って存在し、マントルから押し上がるマグマによって新しい地殻が作られる。 [13][14]

最もよく知られた発散境界である中央大西洋海嶺の拡大率は平均で年2.5センチメートル、100万年で25キロメートルに相当し、過去1〜2億年の海底拡大が大西洋をヨーロッパ・アフリカ・南北アメリカの間の小さな入り江から現在の巨大な大洋へ成長させた。 [15][16]

収束境界ではプレートが互いに向かい合い、一方のプレートが沈み込む場所は沈み込み帯と呼ばれる。地球の大きさは過去6億年間でほとんど変わっていないため、地殻は生成とほぼ同じ速度で破壊される。海洋プレート同士の収束が作る海溝では、マリアナ海溝南端のチャレンジャー海淵が約11,000メートルに達し、エベレストの海抜約8,854メートルよりも深く地球内部へ入り込む。 [17][20]

大陸同士の衝突ではどちらのプレートも沈み込まず、地殻が屈曲して押し上げられる。約5,000万年前に始まったインドのアジアへの衝突はヒマラヤとチベット高原を押し上げた。沈み込み帯では大地震も発生し、1994年6月9日にはボリビアのラパス北東約320キロ、深さ636キロでマグニチュード8.3の地震が発生している。 [18][19]

2枚のプレートが水平にすれ違う帯域はトランスフォーム断層境界と呼ばれ、この概念はカナダの地球物理学者J・トゥーゾ・ウィルソンに始まる。トランスフォーム断層の多くは海底にあるが、陸上では長さ約1,300キロのサンアンドレアス断層帯がカリフォルニアの3分の2を貫き、太平洋プレートは北アメリカプレートの横を1,000万年にわたり年平均約5センチメートルの速さでずれ続けてきた。 [21]

## 運動の速度と測定

プレート分離の平均速度は場所によって大きく異なり、北極海嶺が最も遅く年2.5センチメートル未満、チリの西約3,400キロの南太平洋に位置する東太平洋海膨が最も速く年15センチメートル超である。 [22]

現在のプレート運動はVLBI（超長基線干渉法）・衛星レーザー測距・GPSという宇宙測地技術で直接追跡でき、数年間平均した運動の速度と方向は数百万年間の平均とよく一致することがデータで確認されている。 [23]

## プレート内部の火山と未解決の問題

地震と火山噴火の大半はプレート境界近くで起こるが、ハワイ諸島は全体が火山成因でありながら最近のプレート境界から3,200キロ以上離れた太平洋中央に位置する例外である。1963年にウィルソンが考案した「ホットスポット」理論は、ハワイ諸島・天皇海山群の直線形を、太平洋プレートがマントル内の深い定常ホットスポット上を移動した結果と説明する。 [24][25]

この説に従えば、プレート移動で島は熱源から運ばれて火山活動を失い、ホットスポット上では別の島が成長する。最も北西の有人島カウアイ島の最古の火山岩は約550万年前で深く浸食されているのに対し、ホットスポット上にあるとされるハワイ島の露出岩石は70万年未満で、新しい火山岩が形成され続けている。過去1,000万年間に地殻の下で100以上のホットスポットが活動したと考えられ、イエローストーンでは想定されるホットスポットの熱エネルギーが1万を超える熱水鉱泉・間欠泉・泥沸泉を賄う。 [26][27][28]

ただし、冊子の刊行後もホットスポットをめぐる活発な議論が続き、新しい研究はホットスポットが深部現象でも位置が固定されたものでもないと示唆している。プレートテクトニクスに似た過程が[太陽系](/hubpedia/solar-system)の他の惑星で働くか、働いたことがあるかも議論の対象である。 [29][12]

en.title: Plate tectonics
en.summary: Plate tectonics is the theory that the Earth's outermost layer is fragmented into a dozen or more large and small rigid plates that move relative to one another while riding atop hotter, more mobile material. Motions along divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries explain earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain building; the theory grew out of Wegener's 1912 continental drift hypothesis and was established in the 1960s.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## The theory of plate tectonics

In geologic terms, a plate is a large, rigid slab of solid rock, and the word tectonics comes from the Greek root "to build." The theory of plate tectonics states that the Earth's outermost layer is fragmented into a dozen or more large and small plates that are moving relative to one another as they ride atop hotter, more mobile material. [1][2]

In the picture this theory inherited, the supercontinent Pangaea began to break up about 225-200 million years ago, eventually fragmenting into the continents as we know them today. Plate tectonics has unified the study of the Earth by drawing together many branches of the earth sciences, from paleontology to seismology, and it provided explanations for why [earthquakes](/hubpedia/earthquake) and [volcanic](/hubpedia/volcano) eruptions occur in very specific areas around the world and how great mountain ranges formed. [3][10]

## From continental drift to plate tectonics

The belief that continents have not always been fixed in their present positions was first suggested as early as 1596 by the Dutch map maker Abraham Ortelius in his work Thesaurus Geographicus. It was not until 1912 that the idea of moving continents was seriously considered as a full-blown scientific theory, when a 32-year-old German meteorologist named Alfred Lothar Wegener published the continental drift hypothesis in two articles. [4][5]

Wegener regarded the presence of identical fossil species along the coastal parts of South America and Africa as the most compelling evidence that the two continents were once joined, and further support came from fossils of tropical plants found as coal deposits in Antarctica and from glacial deposits in present-day arid Africa. [6]

A fatal weakness in Wegener's theory was that it could not satisfactorily answer what kind of forces could be strong enough to move such large masses of solid rock over such great distances, and the English geophysicist Harold Jeffreys argued correctly that it was physically impossible for a large mass of solid rock to plow through the ocean floor without breaking up. Wegener froze to death in 1930 during an expedition crossing the Greenland ice cap, but the controversy he spawned raged on, and new evidence from ocean floor exploration rekindled interest in his theory after his death, ultimately leading to the theory of plate tectonics. [7][8]

Plate tectonics has proven to be as important to the earth sciences as the discovery of the structure of the atom was to physics and chemistry and the theory of evolution was to the life sciences. Yet the nature of the forces propelling the plates, the question Wegener failed to resolve, remains one of the chief outstanding questions today. [9][11]

## The four types of plate boundaries

Most movement occurs along narrow zones between plates, and there are four types of plate boundaries: divergent, convergent, transform, and plate boundary zones. Divergent boundaries occur along spreading centers where plates are moving apart and new crust is created by magma pushing up from the mantle. [13][14]

The rate of spreading along the best-known divergent boundary, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, averages about 2.5 centimeters per year, or 25 km in a million years, and seafloor spreading over the past 100 to 200 million years has caused the Atlantic Ocean to grow from a tiny inlet of water between the continents of Europe, Africa, and the Americas into the vast ocean that exists today. [15][16]

At convergent boundaries plates move toward each other, and the location where a plate sinks beneath another is called a subduction zone. Because the size of the Earth has not changed significantly during the past 600 million years, crust must be destroyed at about the same rate as it is being created. Among the trenches formed where oceanic plates converge, the Challenger Deep at the southern end of the Marianas Trench plunges nearly 11,000 m into the Earth's interior, deeper than Mount Everest's roughly 8,854 m above sea level. [17][20]

When two continents meet head-on, neither is subducted because the continental rocks are relatively light; instead the crust buckles and is pushed upward. The collision of India into Asia 50 million years ago crumpled the collision zone and pushed up the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau. Subduction zones also produce great earthquakes: on 9 June 1994, a magnitude-8.3 earthquake struck about 320 km northeast of La Paz, Bolivia, at a depth of 636 km. [18][19]

The zone between two plates sliding horizontally past one another is called a transform-fault boundary, a concept that originated with the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson. Most transform faults are found on the ocean floor, but on land the San Andreas fault zone, about 1,300 km long, slices through two thirds of the length of California, along which the Pacific Plate has been grinding horizontally past the North American Plate for 10 million years at an average rate of about 5 cm per year. [21]

## Rates of motion and how they are measured

Average rates of plate separation range widely: the Arctic Ridge has the slowest rate at less than 2.5 cm per year, and the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island, about 3,400 km west of Chile in the South Pacific, has the fastest at more than 15 cm per year. [22]

Current plate movement can be tracked directly by the space-geodetic techniques of very long baseline interferometry, satellite laser ranging, and the Global Positioning System, and space-geodetic data have confirmed that the rates and direction of plate movement averaged over several years compare well with those averaged over millions of years. [23]

## Volcanoes inside plates and open questions

The vast majority of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur near plate boundaries, but the Hawaiian Islands are an exception: entirely of volcanic origin, they formed in the middle of the Pacific Ocean more than 3,200 km from the nearest plate boundary. The hotspot theory devised by Wilson in 1963 explains the distinctive linear shape of the Hawaiian Island-Emperor Seamounts chain as the result of the Pacific Plate moving over a deep, stationary hotspot in the mantle. [24][25]

On that account, plate movement carries each island beyond the hotspot so volcanism ceases, while another island develops over the hotspot. The oldest volcanic rocks on Kauai, the northwesternmost inhabited Hawaiian island, are about 5.5 million years old and deeply eroded, whereas on the Big Island of Hawaii, presumably still positioned over the hotspot, the oldest exposed rocks are less than 0.7 million years old and new volcanic rock is continually being formed. More than a hundred hotspots beneath the Earth's crust are thought to have been active during the past 10 million years, and at Yellowstone the thermal energy of the presumed hotspot fuels more than 10,000 hot pools and springs, geysers, and bubbling mudpots. [26][27][28]

Vigorous scientific debate about hotspots has continued since the booklet's publication, and new studies suggest that hotspots are neither deep phenomena nor fixed in position over geologic time. Whether processes similar to plate tectonics operate, or have ever operated, on other planets in our [solar system](/hubpedia/solar-system) is also debated. [29][12]

title: 氷河
summary: 氷河は、長年にわたり降り積もった雪が圧縮されて大きく厚い氷の塊となり、自重と重力でゆっくり流動する陸上の氷体である。現在は世界の陸地の約10％を覆い、水循環では海洋に次ぐ第2の水の貯留層であり、気泡を閉じ込めた氷は過去の気候の記録としても利用される。
bodyMarkdown:
## 氷河の形成と構造

氷河は、長年にわたって降り積もった雪が圧縮されて大きく厚い氷の塊となることでできる。圧縮された雪が溶けずに残れば、やがて氷河氷となり氷河へと変わる。 [1][2]

陸上の比較的恒久的な氷の形成物が氷河であるのに対し、氷山は水上の比較的短命な自由浮遊氷体であり、多くは氷河から氷塊が裂け落ちてできる。 [10]

## 流動と進退

氷河はその巨大な質量のため、ごく遅い川のように流れる。氷河の上面は底面より速く動き、底面は地面の表面との摩擦で減速される。 [3][4]

十分に長い期間に多量の[降水](/hubpedia/precipitation)（降雪）が積もれば氷河の質量は増えて前進し、十分に長い期間の温暖な気温は氷河の氷と雪の融解を増やして後退させる。一部の氷河は数週間から数か月にわたり1日数メートルの速さで急進（サージ）することがあり、1986年にはアラスカのハバード氷河が1日10メートル（32フィート）の速さで急進し、わずか2か月でラッセルフィヨルドの水を堰き止めて湖を作った。 [5][6]

## 規模、分布と氷期サイクル

現在、氷河は世界の陸地総面積の約10％を占め、大半は南極・グリーンランド・カナダ北極圏などの極域に分布する。最終氷期には氷が陸地の約32％、海洋の約30％を覆っており、今日の氷河はその名残とみなせる。 [7][8]

過去75万年以内には、間氷期と呼ばれる温暖期で隔てられた8回の氷期サイクルがあったことが分かっている。[水循環](/hubpedia/water-cycle)において、氷河の氷は海洋に次ぐ第2の水の貯留層である。 [9][22]

## 気候記録としての氷河

氷河氷の年代は数百年から数十万年に及び、長期的な気候記録を読むために科学者は氷河や氷床からアイスコアを掘削する。氷河はアイスコアの小さな気泡の中に数千年前の大気の断片を保存し、過去の大気の状態・気温変動・植生の型を明らかにする。 [11][12]

この種の研究を支えるため、米国国立雪氷データセンター（NSIDC）の世界氷河目録は13万を超える氷河の情報を収録している。 [15]

## 後退と水資源

20世紀初頭以来、ほとんど例外なく世界中の氷河が前例のない速さで後退している。アラスカのミューア氷河は60年余りで7マイル（12キロメートル）以上後退し、800メートル（2,600フィート）以上薄くなった。 [13][14]

山岳氷河、特にアラスカの氷河は、海面水位の上昇とその世界的影響に大きく寄与する。海に届く前に氷河の融水は人間の飲料・農業・レクリエーション・水力発電に淡水を供給し、夏期後半の融水放出は春の融雪と秋の雨の間の河川流量を維持する。氷河は下流の生態系と生物学的に結びつき、サケに不可欠な冷水を供給し、融水は[表層流出](/hubpedia/surface-runoff)として下流へ運ばれる。 [16][21][17][18]

変化を追跡するため、米国地質調査所は気候的に異なる地域を代表する中〜高緯度の5つのベンチマーク氷河サイトを設け、科学者が毎年春と秋に同じサイトを訪れて降雪量と雪氷の融解を直接測定している。 [19][20]

en.title: Glacier
en.summary: A glacier is a land-based ice mass formed when snow accumulated over many years compresses into a large, thickened body of ice that moves slowly under its own weight and gravity. Glaciers currently cover about ten percent of the world's land area, hold the second largest reservoir of water in the water cycle after the oceans, and their air-bubble-trapping ice serves as a record of past climate.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Formation and structure of glaciers

Glaciers are made up of fallen snow that, over many years, compresses into large, thickened ice masses. Over time and as more snow falls, if the compressed snow doesn't melt, the snow eventually becomes glacial ice, transforming into a glacier. [1][2]

While a glacier is a relatively permanent ice formation on land, an iceberg is a comparatively short-lived free-floating body of ice on water, and icebergs typically form when chunks of ice break off of a glacier. [10]

## Flow, advance, and retreat

Due to their sheer mass, glaciers flow like very slow rivers. The top of the glacier moves faster than the underside because the underside is slowed by the friction created as it slides along the ground's surface. [3][4]

Greater amounts of snowfall accumulating as [precipitation](/hubpedia/precipitation) over a long enough time will add to the mass of a glacier, causing it to advance, while warmer temperatures over a long enough time result in more of the glacier's ice and snow melting, causing it to retreat. Some glaciers may surge, racing forward at several meters per day for weeks or even months; in 1986 the Hubbard Glacier in Alaska surged at the rate of 10 meters (32 feet) per day, and in only two months the glacier dammed water in the Russell Fjord and created a lake. [5][6]

## Extent, distribution, and ice age cycles

Today, glaciers occupy about ten percent of the world's total land area, with most located in polar regions like Antarctica, Greenland, and the Canadian Arctic. Glaciers can be thought of as remnants from the last Ice Age, when ice covered nearly 32 percent of the land and 30 percent of the oceans. [7][8]

Within the past 750,000 years there have been eight Ice Age cycles separated by warmer periods called interglacial periods. In the [water cycle](/hubpedia/water-cycle), glacier ice is the second largest reservoir of water after the oceans. [9][22]

## Glaciers as climate records

Glacial ice can range in age from several hundred to several hundreds of thousands of years old, and to see a long-term climate record scientists drill and extract ice cores from glaciers and ice sheets. Glaciers preserve bits of atmosphere from thousands of years ago in tiny air bubbles trapped within the ice cores, which can reveal past atmospheric conditions, temperature variations, and types of vegetation. [11][12]

Supporting this kind of research, the World Glacier Inventory maintained by the National Snow and Ice Data Center contains information for over 130,000 glaciers. [15]

## Retreat and water resources

Since the early twentieth century, with few exceptions, glaciers around the world have been retreating at unprecedented rates. Alaska's Muir Glacier retreated by more than seven miles (12 kilometers) and thinned by more than 800 meters (2,600 feet) in a span of just over 60 years. [13][14]

Mountain glaciers, particularly in Alaska, contribute significantly to sea level rise and its global implications. Before reaching the sea, glacier melt provides freshwater for human consumption, agriculture, recreation, and hydropower, and meltwater released during the late summer season sustains streamflow between spring snow melt and fall rain. Glaciers are biologically linked to their downstream ecosystems, providing cold water critical for salmon, and the melt is carried downstream as [surface runoff](/hubpedia/surface-runoff). [16][21][17][18]

To track these changes, the U.S. Geological Survey operates five Benchmark Glacier sites spanning mid to high latitudes and representing climatically distinct regions from inland to coastal, and scientists visit the same sites every spring and fall to make direct measurements of snow accumulation and snow and ice melt. [19][20]

title: 地すべり
summary: 地すべりは、岩・土壌・人工の盛土・デブリまたはその組み合わせが重力で斜面を下方・外方へ移動する広範な過程群である。水による斜面飽和が主原因で、地震・浸食・火山活動・人間の工事などが誘因となり、墜落・転倒・滑動・拡散・流動の様式をとる。野火の焼け跡では少量の雨でもデブリフローが発生しうる。
bodyMarkdown:
## 地すべりとは

地すべりという用語は、岩・土壌・人工の盛土またはこれらの組み合わせを含む斜面構成材料の下方・外方への移動をもたらす、広範な過程群を表す。材料は墜落・転倒・滑動・拡散・流動によって動きうる。 [1][2]

地すべりは主に山岳地域と結びつけられるが、起伏の少ない地域でも道路や建物の掘削による切土・盛土の破壊、河岸の崩壊、側方拡散、鉱山廃滓の崩落などとして発生する。米国では全50州で地すべりが発生し、主な発生・潜在地域はカリフォルニア・オレゴン・ワシントンの沿岸・山岳部、内陸西部の諸州、東部の山岳・丘陵地域で、アラスカとハワイも全種類の地すべりを経験している。 [3][4]

## 地すべりの主な型

狭義の滑落（スライド）は、滑動材料とその下の安定した材料を分ける明確な弱層帯がある塊移動を指し、破断面が上向きに凹んだ回転型と、ほぼ平面に沿って動く並進型が主要な2型である。落石（フォール）は急斜面や崖から分離した岩・巨石の急激な動きで、自由落下・跳ね返り・転がりで移動し、重力・機械的風化・間隙水の存在に強く影響される。転倒（トップル）は、単位内部の低い支点を中心とした前方回転による破壊である。 [6][7][8]

流動（フロー）には5つの基本類型がある。デブリフローは、緩い土・岩・有機物・空気・水がスラリー状になって斜面を下る急速な塊移動で、激しい[降水](/hubpedia/precipitation)や急速な融雪による激しい表層水の流れが急斜面の緩い土や岩を浸食・移動させることで起こる。泥流は少なくとも50％の砂・シルト・粘土粒径の粒子を含む急速に流れるほど湿った土石流で、報道では泥流とデブリフローが「マッドスライド」と呼ばれることも多い。 [9][11]

クリープは、剪断破壊を起こすには小さすぎるが永久変形を生じるのに十分な剪断応力による、知覚できないほど遅い定常的な下方運動で、湾曲した樹幹・曲がった柵・傾いた電柱・小さな土の波状起伏で示される。側方拡散は緩斜面や平坦地で起こり、飽和した緩い非粘性堆積物が固相から液化状態へ変わる液状化が原因で、通常[地震](/hubpedia/earthquake)のような急速な地動が誘因となる。 [12][13]

## 原因と誘因

地すべりの原因は地質的・形態的・人為的に分けられ、世界で最も被害の大きい地すべりを生む3つの要因は水・地震活動・火山活動である。水による斜面飽和は地すべりの主原因で、激しい降雨・融雪・地下水位の変化・海岸線や土ダム・湖沼・溜池・運河・河川の水際の水位変化の形で起こりうる。地すべりと洪水は降水・流出・地盤の水飽和を通じて密接に結びつき、デブリフローや泥流は小さな急な渓流で起こり洪水と誤認されることも多い。 [14][15]

地震は、急で地すべりを起こしやすい地域で発生すると、地すべりの可能性を大きく高める。1964年のグレートアラスカ地震は広範な地すべりと地盤破壊を引き起こし、地震による金銭的損失の大部分を占めた。火山活動による地すべりは最も壊滅的な種類の一つで、[火山](/hubpedia/volcano)の溶岩が雪を急速に溶かして生じる岩・土・灰・水の奔流は急斜面で加速し、ラハールと呼ばれる火山性泥流は火山の裾野を離れても遠距離に達する。1980年のワシントンのセント・ヘレンズ山噴火は、記録史上最大の地すべりを火山の北斜面で誘発した。 [17][18][19]

人為的な原因には、斜面やその麓の掘削、斜面や稜線への載荷、貯水池の水位低下、森林破壊、灌漑、鉱業、人工振動、公益設備からの漏水がある。形態的原因には、斜面裾や側縁の河川・波・[氷河](/hubpedia/glacier)による浸食や、火災・干ばつによる植生除去も含まれる。 [20]

## 影響と規模

米国の地すべりは年間約35億ドル（2001年ドル）の被害と年25〜50人の死者をもたらし、死者は主に落石・岩盤滑落・デブリフローによる。世界では毎年数千人の死傷者と数十億ドルの金銭損失を生じ、長期的な経済混乱・人口移動・自然環境への悪影響を伴うことが多い。地すべりは局地的な問題とみなされがちだが、その影響と費用は自治体の境界を越えて州や国の問題になりうる。 [5][21][22]

地すべりは谷や渓流を堰き止める地すべりダムを形成して大量の水を逆流させ、湛水やダム決壊に伴う下流の洪水を起こしうる。 [16]

## 火災後のデブリフローと軽減

野火の焼け跡の麓や下流は、特に急な地形の近くで鉄砲水とデブリフローに対して弱くなる。焼けた土は舗装路面のように水をはじくため、通常なら吸収される雨が極めて速く流出し、鉄砲水を生むのに必要な雨量がはるかに少なくなる。斜面の植生を失わせる火災はデブリフローへの感受性を高める。 [24][10]

デブリフローは乾いた斜面でも激しい雨が数分続けば始まりうる。ここで「激しい」雨とは速い速度での突発的な雨、およそ1時間に0.5インチ（約1.3センチメートル）を指し、デブリフローでは総雨量より降雨速度が重要である。デブリフローは速く予測不能で、人が走るより速く移動でき、開始位置も進路も正確には予測できない。焼け跡で鉄砲水を生む雨量の目安は1時間未満の0.5インチで、火災の激しさと地形の急さに応じて増減し、焼け跡内の鉄砲水感受性は火災後最初の2年間で最も高い。 [25][26][27]

野火が斜面を焼くと数年間デブリフローの確率が高まり、危険は時間とともにゆっくり低下する。デブリフローを止めたり進路を変えたりすることは誰にもできず、砂袋・暗渠・擁壁は泥と水を誘導できてもデブリフローには通じない。一般に、急斜面や既存の地すべり上の建設を避けるか斜面を安定化させることで地すべりの危険は減らせ、滑動体への地下水の上昇を防ぐと安定性が増す。 [28][29][23]

en.title: Landslide
en.summary: A landslide is the downslope movement of rock, soil, artificial fill, debris, or a combination of these under gravity. Water saturation is a primary cause, while earthquakes, erosion, volcanic activity, and human works act as triggers, and the material may move by falling, toppling, sliding, spreading, or flowing. On wildfire burn scars, even modest rainfall can produce debris flows.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## What a landslide is

The term "landslide" describes a wide variety of processes that result in the downward and outward movement of slope-forming materials including rock, soil, artificial fill, or a combination of these. The materials may move by falling, toppling, sliding, spreading, or flowing. [1][2]

Although landslides are primarily associated with mountainous regions, they can also occur in areas of generally low relief, for example as cut-and-fill failures at roadway and building excavations, river bluff failures, lateral spreads, and collapse of mine-waste piles. In the United States, landslides occur in all 50 States; the primary regions of occurrence and potential are the coastal and mountainous areas of California, Oregon, and Washington, the intermountain west, and the mountainous and hilly regions of the East, while Alaska and Hawaii experience all types of landslides. [3][4]

## The main types of landslide

In the narrower sense, a slide is a mass movement with a distinct zone of weakness separating the slide material from more stable underlying material, and the two major types are rotational slides, whose rupture surface is curved concavely upward, and translational slides, which move along a roughly planar surface. Falls are abrupt movements of masses of geologic materials such as rocks and boulders detached from steep slopes or cliffs, moving by free-fall, bouncing, and rolling under the strong influence of gravity, mechanical weathering, and interstitial water. Toppling failures involve the forward rotation of a unit about a pivotal point low within it. [6][7][8]

Flows fall into five basic categories. A debris flow is a rapid mass movement in which loose soil, rock, organic matter, air, and water mobilize as a slurry flowing downslope, commonly caused by intense surface-water flow from heavy [precipitation](/hubpedia/precipitation) or rapid snowmelt that erodes and mobilizes loose soil or rock on steep slopes. A mudflow is an earthflow wet enough to flow rapidly and containing at least 50 percent sand-, silt-, and clay-sized particles, and in many news reports mudflows and debris flows are commonly called "mudslides." [9][11]

Creep is the imperceptibly slow, steady, downward movement of slope-forming soil or rock, caused by shear stress sufficient to produce permanent deformation but too small to produce shear failure, and it is indicated by curved tree trunks, bent fences or retaining walls, tilted poles, and small soil ripples. Lateral spreads usually occur on very gentle slopes or flat terrain; the failure is caused by liquefaction, in which saturated, loose, cohesionless sediments are transformed from a solid into a liquefied state, and it is usually triggered by rapid ground motion such as that experienced during an [earthquake](/hubpedia/earthquake). [12][13]

## Causes and triggers

Landslide causes are grouped as geological, morphological, and human, and the three that produce most of the world's damaging landslides are water, seismic activity, and volcanic activity. Slope saturation by water is a primary cause, occurring as intense rainfall, snowmelt, changes in ground-water levels, and water-level changes along coastlines, earth dams, and the banks of lakes, reservoirs, canals, and rivers. Landsliding and flooding are closely allied because both relate to precipitation, runoff, and the saturation of ground by water, and debris flows and mudflows, which usually occur in small, steep stream channels, are often mistaken for floods. [14][15]

Earthquakes in steep landslide-prone areas greatly increase the likelihood that landslides will occur. The 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake caused widespread landsliding and other ground failure, which caused most of the monetary loss due to the earthquake. Landslides due to volcanic activity are some of the most devastating: lava from a [volcano](/hubpedia/volcano) may melt snow at a rapid rate, causing a deluge of rock, soil, ash, and water that accelerates on steep volcanic slopes, and these volcanic debris flows, known as lahars, reach great distances once they leave the flanks. The 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens in Washington triggered a massive landslide on the volcano's north flank, the largest landslide in recorded times. [17][18][19]

Human causes include excavation of a slope or its toe, loading of a slope or its crest, reservoir drawdown, deforestation, irrigation, mining, artificial vibration, and water leakage from utilities. Morphological causes include fluvial, wave, or [glacial](/hubpedia/glacier) erosion of a slope toe or lateral margins, and vegetation removal by fire or drought. [20]

## Impacts and scale

In the United States, landslides cause approximately $3.5 billion (year 2001 dollars) in damage and kill between 25 and 50 people annually, with casualties primarily caused by rockfalls, rock slides, and debris flows. Worldwide, landslides occur under all climatic conditions and terrains, cost billions in monetary losses, and are responsible for thousands of deaths and injuries each year, often causing long-term economic disruption, population displacement, and negative effects on the natural environment. Landslides are often characterized as local problems, but their effects and costs frequently cross local jurisdictions and may become state or national problems. [5][21][22]

Landslides can also cause flooding by forming landslide dams that block valleys and stream channels, allowing large amounts of water to back up and producing backwater flooding and, if the dam fails, subsequent downstream flooding. [16]

## Post-fire debris flows and mitigation

Locations downhill and downstream from burned areas are very susceptible to flash flooding and debris flows, especially near steep terrain. Rainfall that would normally be absorbed runs off extremely quickly after a wildfire, because burned soil can be as water-repellant as pavement, so much less rainfall is required to produce a flash flood. Fires that denude slopes of vegetation intensify the susceptibility of slopes to debris flows. [24][10]

A debris flow can start on a dry slope after only a few minutes of intense rain, where "intense" means a burst of rain at a fast rate, about half an inch in an hour; with debris flows, the rainfall rate matters more than total rainfall. Debris flows are fast and unpredictable — they can travel faster than a person can run, and no one can say precisely where one will start or where it will go. A general rule of thumb is that half an inch of rainfall in less than an hour is sufficient to cause flash flooding in a burn area, though this varies with fire severity and terrain steepness, and susceptibility within the burned area is greatest during the first two years following the fire. [25][26][27]

When a wildfire burns a slope, it increases the chance of debris flows for several years, though the danger slowly drops over time. No one can stop a debris flow or change its path; sandbags, culverts, and retaining walls can help redirect mud and water, but not debris flows. In general, the hazard from landslides can be reduced by avoiding construction on steep slopes and existing landslides or by stabilizing the slopes, and stability increases when ground water is prevented from rising in the landslide mass. [28][29][23]

evidence.quote: Toppling failures are distinguished by the forward rotation of a unit or units about some pivotal point, below or low in the unit, under the actions of gravity and forces exerted by adjacent units or by fluids in cracks

claims.statement: デブリフローは緩い土・岩・有機物・空気・水がスラリー状になって斜面を下る急速な塊移動で、激しい降水や急速な融雪による表層水流が急斜面の緩い土や岩を浸食・移動させることで起こる。

evidence.quote: A debris flow is a form of rapid mass movement in which a combination of loose soil, rock, organic matter, air, and water mobilize as a slurry that flows downslope
Debris flows are commonly caused by intense surface-water flow, due to heavy precipitation or rapid snowmelt, that erodes and mobilizes loose soil or rock on steep slopes.

claims.statement: 斜面の植生を失わせる火災は、デブリフローへの感受性を高める。

evidence.quote: Fires that denude slopes of vegetation intensify the susceptibility of slopes to debris flows.

claims.statement: 泥流は少なくとも50％の砂・シルト・粘土粒径の粒子を含む急速に流れるほど湿った土石流であり、泥流とデブリフローは報道で「マッドスライド」と呼ばれることも多い。

evidence.quote: A mudflow is an earthflow consisting of material that is wet enough to flow rapidly and that contains at least 50 percent sand-, silt-, and clay-sized particles.
mudflows and debris flows are commonly referred to as "mudslides."

claims.statement: クリープは、永久変形を生じるのに十分だが剪断破壊には小さすぎる剪断応力による知覚できないほど遅い定常的な下方運動で、湾曲した樹幹・曲がった柵・傾いた電柱・小さな土の波状起伏で示される。

evidence.quote: Creep is the imperceptibly slow, steady, downward movement of slope-forming soil or rock. Movement is caused by shear stress sufficient to produce permanent deformation, but too small to produce shear failure.
Creep is indicated by curved tree trunks, bent fences or retaining walls, tilted poles or fences, and small soil ripples or ridges

claims.statement: 側方拡散は緩斜面や平坦地で起こり、飽和した緩い非粘性堆積物が固相から液化状態へ変わる液状化が原因で、通常地震のような急速な地動が誘因となる。

evidence.quote: The failure is caused by liquefaction, the process whereby saturated, loose, cohesionless sediments (usually sands and silts) are transformed from a solid into a liquefied state. Failure is usually triggered by rapid ground motion, such as that experienced during an earthquake, but can also be artificially induced.

claims.statement: 水による斜面飽和は地すべりの主原因であり、激しい降雨・融雪・地下水位の変化・海岸線や土ダム・湖沼・溜池・運河・河川の水際の水位変化の形で起こりうる。

evidence.quote: Slope saturation by water is a primary cause of landslides. This effect can occur in the form of intense rainfall, snowmelt, changes in ground-water levels, and water-level changes along coastlines, earth dams, and the banks of lakes, reservoirs, canals, and rivers.

claims.statement: 地すべりと洪水は降水・流出・地盤の水飽和を通じて密接に結びつき、小さな急な渓流で起こるデブリフローや泥流は洪水と誤認されることが多い。

evidence.quote: Landsliding and flooding are closely allied because both are related to precipitation, runoff, and the saturation of ground by water. In addition, debris flows and mudflows usually occur in small, steep stream channels and often are mistaken for floods; in fact, these two events often occur simultaneously in the same area.

claims.statement: 地すべりは谷や渓流を堰き止める地すべりダムを形成して湛水を生じ、ダムが決壊すれば下流の洪水を起こす。

evidence.quote: Landslides can cause flooding by forming landslide dams that block valleys and stream channels, allowing large amounts of water to back up.

claims.statement: 急で地すべりを起こしやすい地域での地震は地すべりの可能性を大きく高め、1964年のグレートアラスカ地震は広範な地すべりと地盤破壊を起こして地震の金銭的損失の大部分を占めた。

evidence.quote: The occurrence of earthquakes in steep landslide-prone areas greatly increases the likelihood that landslides will occur
The 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake caused widespread landsliding and other ground failure, which caused most of the monetary loss due to the earthquake.

claims.statement: 火山活動による地すべりは最も壊滅的な種類の一つで、溶岩が雪を急速に溶かして生じる岩・土・灰・水の奔流は火山の急斜面で加速し、ラハールと呼ばれる火山性泥流は裾野を離れても遠距離に達する。

evidence.quote: Landslides due to volcanic activity are some of the most devastating types. Volcanic lava may melt snow at a rapid rate, causing a deluge of rock, soil, ash, and water that accelerates rapidly on the steep slopes of volcanoes
These volcanic debris flows (also known as lahars) reach great distances, once they leave the flanks of the volcano

claims.statement: 1980年のワシントンのセント・ヘレンズ山噴火は、火山の北斜面で記録史上最大の地すべりを誘発した。

evidence.quote: The 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, in Washington triggered a massive landslide on the north flank of the volcano, the largest landslide in recorded times.

claims.statement: 人為的原因には斜面やその麓の掘削・載荷・貯水池の水位低下・森林破壊・灌漑・鉱業・人工振動・漏水があり、形態的原因には河川・波・氷河による斜面裾の浸食や火災・干ばつによる植生除去が含まれる。

evidence.quote: a. Excavation of slope or its toe
b. Loading of slope or its crest
d. Deforestation
e. Irrigation
c. Fluvial, wave, or glacial erosion of slope toe or lateral margins
f. Vegetation removal (by fire, drought)

claims.statement: 地すべりは世界中のあらゆる気候・地形条件で発生し、毎年数十億ドルの金銭損失と数千人の死傷をもたらし、長期的な経済混乱・人口移動・自然環境への悪影響を伴うことが多い。

evidence.quote: Landslides occur throughout the world, under all climatic conditions and terrains, cost billions in monetary losses, and are responsible for thousands of deaths and injuries each year. Often, they cause long-term economic disruption, population displacement, and negative effects on the natural environment.

claims.statement: 地すべりは局地的な問題とみなされがちだが、その影響と費用は地方自治体の境界を越えて州や国の問題になりうる。

evidence.quote: Landslides often are characterized as local problems, but their effects and costs frequently cross local jurisdictions and may become State or Provincial or national problems.

claims.statement: 急斜面や既存の地すべり上の建設を避けるか斜面を安定化させることで地すべりの危険は減らせ、滑動体への地下水の上昇を防ぐと安定性が増す。

evidence.quote: The hazard from landslides can be reduced by avoiding construction on steep slopes and existing landslides, or by stabilizing the slopes. Stability increases when ground water is prevented from rising in the landslide mass

claims.statement: 焼け跡の麓や下流は特に急な地形の近くで鉄砲水とデブリフローに弱く、焼けた土は舗装路面のように水をはじくため通常吸収される雨が極めて速く流出する。

evidence.quote: Locations downhill and downstream from burned areas are very susceptible to Flash Flooding and Debris Flows, especially near steep terrain. Rainfall that would normally be absorbed will run off extremely quickly after a wildfire, as burned soil can be as water-repellant as pavement.

claims.statement: デブリフローは乾いた斜面でも激しい雨が数分続けば始まりうる。「激しい」雨とは約1時間に0.5インチの速い降雨で、総雨量より降雨速度が重要である。

evidence.quote: It can start on a dry slope after only a few minutes of intense rain.
"Intense” rain means a burst of rain at a fast rate, about half an inch in an hour. With debris flows, the rainfall rate matters more than total rainfall.

claims.statement: デブリフローは速く予測不能で、人が走るより速く移動でき、開始位置も進路も正確には予測できない。

evidence.quote: Debris flows are fast and unpredictable. They can travel faster than you can run - and they can catch up to your car! Also, no one can say precisely where a debris flow will start or where it will go.

claims.statement: 焼け跡で鉄砲水を生む雨量の目安は1時間未満の0.5インチで、火災の激しさと地形の急さに応じて増減し、焼け跡内の感受性は火災後最初の2年間で最も高い。

evidence.quote: A general rule of thumb is that half an inch of rainfall in less than an hour is sufficient to cause Flash Flooding in a burn area, but this can be more or less depending on the factors above.
The susceptibility to flash flood within the burned area is greatest during the first two years following the fire.

claims.statement: 野火が斜面を焼くと数年間デブリフローの確率が高まり、危険は時間とともにゆっくり低下する。

evidence.quote: When a wildfire burns a slope, it increases the chance of debris flows for several years. The danger does slowly drop over time.

claims.statement: デブリフローを止めたり進路を変えたりすることは誰にもできず、砂袋・暗渠・擁壁は泥と水を誘導できてもデブリフローには通じない。

evidence.quote: No one can stop a debris flow or change its path.
These can help redirect mud and water, but not debris flows.
